edges.relationship: Wedgwood names Marc Bloch among the historians who influenced her historical practice.
edges.evidence_note: Own signed 1960 essay, printed 6, column 1, opening paragraph. Her explicit retrospective acknowledgment names several historians and gives Burckhardt the strongest emphasis; it does not identify a particular Bloch book, doctrine or personal encounter. The original works named elsewhere in the essay remain unread.

edges.relationship: Stone criticizes Wedgwood’s regicide narrative for insufficient political explanation and dramatic reconstruction that, in his judgment, distorts the evidence.
edges.evidence_note: Complete signed original 1964 review, paragraphs beginning “One wonders”, “How far”, “If Miss Wedgwood”, and “The objection”. Stone praises her narrative skill while questioning treatment of the Army, the regicides and the execution’s consequences. These are his criticisms of A Coffin for King Charles, not independently verified errors or a rejection of every narrative history. The reviewed book and archival evidence remain unread.

edges.relationship: Mokyr relates his propositional/prescriptive knowledge distinction to Ryle’s knowing-that and knowing-how.
edges.evidence_note: Own February 2002 draft, printed 4, note 4, explicitly places the distinction beside Ryle (1949), while also crediting Scheffler, Michael Polanyi and Loasby. This is Mokyr’s bounded conceptual analogy, not evidence of formal teaching, sole derivation from Ryle, or identity between the frameworks. The bibliography identifies The Concept of Mind in a Chicago manifestation; neither that original nor the cited intermediaries was newly read. The actual PDF footnote was visually checked; its text-layer rendering of the Greek symbols is unreliable.

edges.relationship: Mokyr uses Burke’s history of the rise of research to connect Enlightenment knowledge with economic and social reform.
edges.evidence_note: Own 2007 lecture, 4–5, explicitly invokes Burke (2000:44) for the emergence of research and its reforming purpose, within Mokyr’s account of Baconian programs. The bibliography at 19 identifies A Social History of Knowledge. This is a particular supporting historical resource, not a claim that Burke supplied the entire useful-knowledge theory, personal contact, or fresh reading of Burke’s book. Bacon, Newton and the joint Jacob–Stewart study retain their distinct roles.

edges.relationship: Mokyr challenges material priority over ideas as a sufficient explanation of eighteenth-century economic change.
edges.evidence_note: Own 2007 lecture, 2 and note 1, sets his conditional account of beliefs affecting economies against Marx’s 1859 formulation of social being and consciousness. He also criticizes an analogous view in Ekelund and Tollison and contrasts Keynes. This records Mokyr’s specific framing of that causal proposition, not a verdict on all of Marx, proof that Marx denied every causal role for ideas, or a newly read Marx original. Mokyr explicitly says the answer depends on circumstances and that correlation between Enlightenment exposure and later growth is insufficient proof.

edges.relationship: Mokyr invokes Braudel for the limits of preindustrial growth spurts when explaining the shift to sustained growth.
edges.evidence_note: Own October 2002 draft, 5, explicitly names Braudel (1981) and Eric Jones as historians who had emphasized growth reaching new stationary states. The bibliography identifies the 1981 English Structures of Everyday Life manifestation. Mokyr uses this resource before modeling negative feedback and diminishing returns; he does not deny all earlier growth. The passage does not establish personal influence, general agreement with Braudel’s capitalism account, or fresh reading of the original book.

edges.relationship: Mokyr uses Wrigley’s account of classical political economy to frame the constraints on preindustrial growth.
edges.evidence_note: Own October 2002 draft, 5, cites Wrigley (1987, 1988) for the constrained growth implicit in British classical political economy before developing his negative-feedback account. The bibliography identifies People, Cities, and Wealth and Continuity, Chance and Change. This particular resource differs from his qualified discussion of coal at 2 and from the preserved opposite arrow edge_2624, where Wrigley uses Mokyr’s illustrative sector model. No wholesale adoption, personal mentorship or fresh reading of either Wrigley book follows.

edges.relationship: Mokyr argues that Wong leaves the intellectual foundations of technological divergence insufficiently explained.
edges.evidence_note: Own October 2002 draft, 2–4, describes Wong’s comparison as unresolved, then criticizes the absence of Needham from China Transformed and demands fuller explanation of useful knowledge and technological change. At 4 he also agrees with Wong that Smithian growth alone cannot explain the transformation. Wong’s book is not newly read or independently audited here; this is Mokyr’s attributed criticism, distinct from the Pomeranz coal-and-land criticism already on edge_1110. The preliminary conference draft is not equated with a published book or proof of conference delivery.

verification.note: Complete signed one-page essay read in all three columns, printed 6/PDF leaf 6, from the original magazine publisher’s archive; page visually collated against OCR. wedgwood_woolrych.note: Complete original British Academy memoir 521–534 freshly read, including all 14 notes, with title/portrait leaf distinct. Existing seminar, advice, revaluation, Parker criticism, biographical caveats and cultural placements remain intact. Schiller’s and Trevelyan’s stronger personal roles are freshly supported by Wedgwood’s own 1960 essay; the memoir alone does not newly establish Bloch’s role. The 1986 Festschrift contributor list does not prove shared doctrine or influence; Woolrych’s 528 polemic is not assigned to Wedgwood. Original prefaces, Parker’s 1984 book and the original 1958 art/science essay remain unread.
